summary: Know your aircraft's checklists, fly the aircraft, assess, then declare an emergency in good time (on 121.5 MHz if not talking to anyone). The call format follows MAYDAY or PAN PAN three times, station, callsign, type, nature, intentions, position, altitude, heading and other information. D&D at London Area Control Centre can give fast position fixes. After engine failure land ahead after take-off and use a constant-aspect approach to a field. Built from the Skyway Code pp.136-141.
src: The Skyway Code (CAP 1535 v4, Nov 2023), pp.136-141
sections: Key principles
Know the AFM checklists for time-critical emergencies by heart
Fly the aircraft: accidents often happen when a non-lethal problem distracts from flying. Keep a safe flying speed
Assess before acting. Do not jump to conclusions
Declare an emergency in good time. It is easier to cancel than to start too late. If not with an ATSU use 121.5 MHz
Select 7700. 'Mayday out' means no reply needed
Mayday and Pan call format
Distress: 'Mayday' three times. Urgency: 'Pan Pan' three times
Then: station addressed, callsign, aircraft type, nature of emergency, intentions, position, altitude, heading, other information (persons on board, pilot qualifications)
There is no ICAO requirement to include pilot qualifications but doing so helps UK controllers
Distress and Diversion Cell (D&D)
The emergency centre at the London Area Control Centre, available 24 hours to pilots in UK airspace in distress or with difficulties such as being unsure of position

Can give accurate position fixes by direction finding. Instant fixes are available in the London FIR at or above 3,000 ft AMSL over land east of Wales and south of Manchester, and in the Scottish FIR at or above 8,500 ft
Also takes practice calls ('Practice PAN' three times) and training fixes if no real emergency is in progress
Lost, comms and electrical failure
Lost: squawk 0030, ask a radar ATSU or call D&D on 121.5, orbit a landmark and do not fly aimlessly
Comms loss: check volume, squelch, frequency and audio panel first, then set 7600, stay in VMC and consider a quiet aerodrome outside CAS. Overhead observe the signal square and light signals
Electrical failure: alternator failure is common and the battery may give about 20 minutes. Reduce load, expect to lose the radio, know which systems are electric (flaps)
Engine failure and field selection
Know your best glide speed and procedure
Shortly after take-off land ahead, rather than turning back
With height check common causes: fuel selection and carb icing
With a partial failure decide positively between a field and an aerodrome
Field choice: wind (into wind), size (bigger), surroundings (power lines), shape (square), surface (grass is better than ploughed fields or crops) and slope (avoid)

Constant aspect approach: enter the pattern, assess the visual angle at about 45°, keep that angle constant by tightening or widening the turn, aim further in if using full flap or gear, and side slip or S-turn if high
Fire and ditching
Fire on the ground: usually when starting. Cut mixture and fuel, keep cranking with the throttle open to draw fire back, otherwise leave upwind
Fire in the air: engine or electrical. Shut down and force land. Do not reset a circuit breaker more than once
Ditching: wear lifejackets (belt over the jacket) and carry a liferaft for significant water crossings. In winter you are unlikely to survive more than an hour immersed unless in a survival suit
